title: Chapter 30 — The Pipe
paragraphs: When Stubb had gone, Ahab stood for a while leaning over the bulwarks. Then, as had been his habit lately, he called a sailor of the watch and sent him below for his ivory stool, and also his pipe. Lighting the pipe at the binnacle lamp (the lamp by the compass) and planting the stool on the weather side of the deck, he sat and smoked.

In old Norse times, the thrones of the sea-loving Danish kings were made, so tradition says, of the tusks of the narwhal. How could anyone look at Ahab then, seated on that tripod of bones, without thinking of the royalty it symbolized? For Ahab was a Khan of the plank, and a king of the sea, and a great lord of Leviathans.

Some moments passed, during which the thick smoke came from his mouth in quick, constant puffs that blew back into his face. "How now," he said to himself at last, taking the stem from his mouth, "this smoking no longer soothes. Oh, my pipe! Things must be going hard with me if your charm is gone! Here I have been unknowingly toiling, not taking pleasure — aye, and ignorantly smoking to windward all the while; to windward, and with such nervous whiffs, as if, like the dying whale, my final spouts were the strongest and fullest of trouble. What business do I have with this pipe? This thing is meant for serenity, to send up mild white vapors among mild white hairs, not among torn iron-gray locks like mine. I'll smoke no more —"

He tossed the still-lit pipe into the sea. The fire hissed in the waves. At the same instant, the ship shot past the bubble the sinking pipe made. With his hat pulled low, Ahab lurched across the planks.
